name: The Guardian
host: GCP VM `trading-1` (europe-west1-b) — there is no Computer 3
duty_cycle: Always on — `s3-ams.service` up 173,153 s at time of writing

status.note: This system is built and running, not designed. `s3-ams.service` is up on `trading-1` in `AMS_MODE=enforce`, and `ams_decision_log` holds **4,153 real decisions** taken between 2026-07-15 and 2026-08-14 — 4,091 rejected, 62 approved at reduced size. All ten gate layers A–J exist in code, plus three the design never had (P, Q, S). 627 of 627 tests pass. It is **not** the blocking link and has not been for five days: a consumer has been pulling `scored_signal_queue_sub` continuously since 2026-08-17. What is blocking the path is upstream and downstream of it — System 1 has published nothing to the topic, and System 2 is bound to the wrong queue file.

summary.technical: System 3 is always-on risk middleware. Every scored signal clears a sequential, short-circuiting decision gate before it can become an order — thirteen layers as built, not ten: `P` provenance, `Q` quarantine, `A` state, `S` account-truth freshness, then `B`–`G`, then sizing, then `H`–`J`. It does arithmetic, not machine learning: account state, loss budgets, drawdown, exposure caps, correlation, quarter-Kelly sizing and calendar windows. It is the only component that sizes a position and it holds no broker credential. Its system of record is **SQLite** (`state/db/ams.db`), not PostgreSQL; Postgres is supported via `DB_PROVIDER=postgres` and has never been provisioned.
summary.plain: System 3 is the risk officer, and it never sleeps. Every trade idea walks past a fixed line of checkpoints in order, and the first one to say no ends it. It is also the only part that decides how much money goes on a trade. It cannot place the trade itself. Two corrections to what was written about it before: there are thirteen checkpoints, not ten, and its memory lives in a simple local file rather than the database the design called for.

technical: **The answer System 1 asked for, in one place.** The subscription is `scored_signal_queue_sub`, on topic `scored_signal_queue`. Both are lowercase. `Scored_Signal_Queue` does not exist in project `scalable-brain` and never has — `gcloud pubsub topics list` returns exactly `AMS_Outbound_Queue`, `AMS_Inbound_Queue`, `scored_signal_queue` and `scored_signal_dlq`. Approved orders are published to the topic `ams-outbound` (`TOPIC_AMS_OUTBOUND`), which the bridge translates onto `ams-outbound.executor` for System 2.

**Yes, a consumer is pulling it right now.** Not `ams.service.main` directly: `s3-signal-relay.service` runs `scripts/pubsub_signal_relay.py`, which pulls `scored_signal_queue_sub`, validates each message against `contracts/v1/ScoredSignal.schema.json`, writes it to the local topic `scored-signals.ams`, and acks **only after** the local write succeeds. Verified two ways — the unit has been up since 2026-08-17, and Cloud Monitoring `pubsub.googleapis.com/subscription/pull_request_count` shows 13,020 successful pulls in the last 24 hours, a flat ~545 per hour, and 55,347 over seven days.

The relay exists because `build_queue()` returns one backend for every topic: flipping System 3 to `pubsub` wholesale would also move its *outbound* leg to `AMS_Outbound_Queue`, where the bridge and System 2 cannot see it, and approved orders would be published and silently never executed. The relay connects the inbound leg only. It has a defined exit — when all three processes move together, delete it and set `SCORED_SIGNAL_SUB=scored_signal_queue_sub`.

Account truth comes from System 2 rather than the broker directly, and the local database is the system of record, written before any approval is published, so a crash cannot lose a decision already acted on.
plain: The exact answers, first. The mailbox is called `scored_signal_queue_sub`, all lower case. The name that was being asked about, with capital letters, does not exist and never did. Approved orders go out to a box called `ams-outbound`.

And yes — somebody is standing at that mailbox right now. A small dedicated program has been checking it every few seconds since 17 August. That is not a claim from a document; the cloud provider's own counters show about 545 checks an hour, without a gap.

It is a separate small program on purpose. Switching the whole risk officer over to the cloud queues would have moved its outgoing post as well, to a box nobody downstream reads — so approvals would have been sent and never delivered. Moving only the incoming leg avoids that.
Everything the risk officer knows about the account is written to its own disk before it acts, so a power cut cannot make it forget a decision it already made.

callouts.title: The zero-runtime-dependency claim is currently false in practice
callouts.technical: The isolation property holds in code — System 3 reads System 1 only as immutable GCS objects. It does not hold in deployment: System 3, System 2, the bridge and the relay are systemd units on one VM. A host failure takes all of them at once, and System 3's SQLite file is on that host's disk. Independent failure domains are a design property that the current deployment does not have.
callouts.plain: On paper the risk officer can keep working if any other machine dies. In reality it is in the same room as everything else, on the same computer. If that computer goes, all three go together.

technical: The decision gate is **sequential and short-circuiting**. The first failure ends evaluation with a logged layer and reason in `ams_decision_log`. The built order is `P, Q, A, S, B, C, D, E, F, G, sizing, H, I, J` — three more layers than the design described, and the letters do not mean what the earlier version of this page said: `H` is the duration/Friday-cutoff check, `I` is the calendar, `J` is final sanity and assembly, and sizing is a distinct step between `G` and `H` rather than a lettered layer.

Every layer is a pure function over already-resolved scalars in `gate/layers.py` — no layer touches the database, the clock or the network, so each is testable to the cent. Missing or unparseable data is coerced default-safe: a non-positive equity yields an infinite exposure so the comparison rejects.
Layer `J` is the only place an approval leaves the system, publishing a fully-sized order to `ams-outbound`. Nothing downstream may adjust that size.

Underneath the gate runs the account state machine — DEMO → ACTIVE → CAUTION → PAUSED → CIRCUIT_BROKEN → RECOVERY — plus the circuit breakers and a deployment ladder (Paper → Micro → Small → Full) whose stage multiplies every position size. The account is in **RECOVERY** at stage **paper** today, which is why 2,719 of the 4,091 rejections are at layer `A`: the guardian is refusing everything, on purpose.
plain: Thirteen checkpoints, in a fixed order, and the first *no* ends the conversation. The cheap questions come first — *is this trade idea's pedigree even legible? is the account allowed to trade today?* — before the system spends effort on the expensive ones.
Twelve of them can only refuse. Exactly one decides the amount. Once that amount is set, nothing downstream may change it.

The account also has a mood, and it changes automatically: healthy, cautious, paused, or shut down. It is currently in recovery at the smallest possible size, which is why the great majority of everything it has ever seen was refused at the very first account-level checkpoint. That is the machinery working, not failing.

stages.name: Strategy provenance
stages.technical: Branches on `selection_basis`: `qualified` full size, `designated` half size logged REDUCED, anything else **including absent** rejects with `unknown_selection_basis`. Runs first, ahead of everything, and its verdict feeds sizing rather than merely passing.
stages.plain: Asks whether the trade idea's pedigree is even readable. A fully proven strategy gets full size, a provisional one gets half, and anything that does not say gets refused outright.

stages.name: Strategy quarantine
stages.technical: Rejects when the signal's `strategy_id` has been quarantined by the decay auditor.
stages.plain: If a strategy has been benched for going bad in live trading, its ideas are refused at the door.

stages.name: Account state + halt
stages.technical: Gate on the state machine and any halt with a future expiry. **2,719 of 4,091 rejections landed here** — the account is in RECOVERY.
stages.plain: Is the account allowed to trade at all right now? For most of this system's life the honest answer has been no.

stages.name: Account-truth freshness
stages.output: Reject on stale snapshot or open book
stages.technical: Runs before B because B is the first layer to read the snapshot-fed account row. A silent outage and a stale value are distinguished in the reason, never merged.
stages.plain: Before deciding on numbers, check the numbers are recent. Deciding on yesterday's balance is worse than not deciding.

stages.name: Daily loss budget
stages.technical: Soft stop halves size and pauses 30 minutes; hard stop halts for 24 hours. Boundaries computed in UTC.
stages.plain: How much has today already cost? Past a point, the day is over.

stages.name: Drawdown guard
stages.technical: Max drawdown from equity peak. Breach transitions to CIRCUIT_BROKEN and closes all positions. Currently 4.85% against a 88,294.53 peak.
stages.plain: How far below the high-water mark is the account? Far enough, and everything closes. It is about a twentieth of the way there.

stages.name: Consecutive losses
stages.technical: Streak counter reset on any win.
stages.plain: Five losses in a row means stop for a day. Usually the market changed, not the luck.

stages.name: Concurrency + trades per day
stages.output: Cap open trades and daily count
stages.technical: Hard caps on simultaneously open positions and on trades initiated per day. 136 rejections here.
stages.plain: No more than a set number of trades open at once, and no more than a set number started in a day.

stages.name: Per-pair exposure
stages.technical: Aggregate risk on a single instrument.
stages.plain: No single currency pair gets more than 6% of the account at risk.

stages.name: Correlated exposure + total heat
stages.output: Max 10% correlated, plus a total cap
stages.technical: Groups correlated instruments and caps aggregate risk across the group and across the whole book.
stages.plain: Prevents taking the same bet five times under five different names — EUR/USD and GBP/USD often move together.

stages.name: Quarter-Kelly sizing
stages.technical: Quarter-Kelly from the strategy's own live edge, capped at 2.0% and floored at 0.1%, then multiplied by state, drawdown, streak, provenance and deployment-stage multipliers. Not a lettered layer, and it can refuse: **1,100 of 4,091 rejections are here**, on insufficient or stale live statistics.
stages.plain: The one step that produces a number instead of a verdict — then deliberately cuts it to a quarter of the mathematically optimal amount, because the maths assumes the edge estimate is perfect and it never is. It also refuses outright when there is not enough live evidence to estimate an edge at all, which is the second most common way a trade dies here.

stages.name: Duration vs Friday cutoff
stages.output: Reject if the hold straddles the weekend
stages.technical: Rejects if holding for the maximum allowed duration would straddle the next Friday cutoff. 131 rejections here.
stages.plain: Do not open a three-day trade on a Friday afternoon.

stages.name: Weekend, holiday, macro
stages.technical: Calendar verdict from `config/holidays.json` and macro windows; a `reduce` verdict feeds the sizing volatility flag, a `reject` is applied here. 5 rejections here.
stages.plain: Stay out of the way of scheduled news, and out of the market on public holidays.

stages.name: Final sanity, assemble, publish
stages.technical: Stop and take-profit on the correct side of entry, positive units, risk within cap and within the tighter RECOVERY cap. The only egress point for an approval.
stages.plain: A last read-through — is the stop actually on the losing side, is the size positive, is the risk inside the cap — then the single door an approved trade leaves by.

callouts.title: Why the guardian is the always-on one
callouts.technical: Risk state is continuous; model building is not. An open position accrues risk every second, so the component tracking it cannot have a duty cycle. System 1 runs weekly, System 2 runs during market hours, System 3 runs forever.
callouts.plain: The research machine can sleep. The trading machine sleeps at weekends. The thing watching your money cannot sleep at all, because the risk does not stop when the office closes.

callouts.title: The latency budget was met by two orders of magnitude
callouts.technical: The design budget was a median under 100 ms. Measured across all 4,153 logged decisions: **0.75 ms mean**, 421 ms maximum. The layers are pure functions over pre-resolved scalars and the orchestrator reads the database once, which is where the margin comes from.
callouts.plain: The target was to decide in under a tenth of a second. It decides in under a thousandth. The rare slow one is a hundredth.

technical: The decay auditor closes the loop: sustained live underperformance quarantines a strategy at layer `Q` and is one of the triggers that can cause System 1 to retrain. That is the only feedback path from live results back into model building, and it is deliberately narrow.

One correction on alerting: `SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_USER` and `SMTP_TO` are all empty in the deployed environment, so the urgency-routed email fallback does not exist. Every alert this system can raise depends on a single Telegram bot token.
plain: There is one thread running back to the research lab: if a strategy stops working in real life, it is benched here and the lab is told to think again. Nothing else about live trading is allowed to influence the research, so the research cannot start fitting itself to recent luck.

A warning about how you would hear from it: the email channel was never filled in. Every alert goes through one Telegram bot. If that bot's token stops working, the risk officer becomes silent without anybody being told.

issues.title: A drill signal, or any new envelope field, is dead-lettered
issues.text: `contracts/v1/ScoredSignal.schema.json` is `additionalProperties: false`. A signal carrying `"drill": true` fails validation at the relay, which by design never acks and never forwards an invalid message — so it retries and dead-letters, and System 1 sees a published message and no response, forever. `ApprovedOrder.schema.json` is also `additionalProperties: false`, so even if the signal were accepted the flag could not be forwarded to System 2. **G-008 cannot run until this is changed.** Layer `P` compounds it: `selection_basis` is optional in the schema but a missing value is a hard REJECT, so a drill signal must carry it.

issues.title: System 2 cannot read what this system publishes
issues.text: Approved orders go to `ams-outbound`, which the bridge translates onto `ams-outbound.executor`. System 2's deployed `QUEUE_LOCAL_PATH` points at a Windows path that resolves to an empty database beside its own source tree, so 5,587 messages have stranded on that topic since 2026-08-20T15:09:24Z. All of them are this system's own heartbeats — no approved order has been lost, because none has been approved since 2026-08-14. The next approval would be. Tracked from System 2's side as GAP-S2-01.

issues.title: Local PostgreSQL is not provisioned — the answer is no
issues.text: `DB_PROVIDER=sqlite`, `DB_PATH=state/db/ams.db`. The `postgresql@18-main` cluster on the host serves System 2's `system2` database only; there is no `ams_db`. Postgres is supported (`DB_PROVIDER=postgres` plus `DB_DSN`) and the migrations exist, but it has never been stood up. SQLite has carried 4,153 decisions without loss, so this is a scale and concurrency concern rather than a correctness one today — but the design called it a hard requirement and it is not met.

issues.title: Every alert depends on one Telegram token
issues.text: `SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_USER` and `SMTP_TO` are blank in the deployed environment. The urgency-routed email fallback described in the design does not exist. A revoked or rate-limited bot token silently removes every channel this system has for telling a human that it has stopped.

issues.title: Nothing has been published to the topic to consume
issues.text: The consumer is live and has been since 2026-08-17. `subscription/sent_message_count` on `scored_signal_queue_sub` is **0** over 24 hours, and `topic/send_request_count` on `scored_signal_queue` shows three publish requests in 25 days, all on 2026-08-17, all of them our own round-trip verification. System 1's task list records the switch from `local` to `pubsub` as done and the producer repair as verified end to end; the topic's own counters do not show a message from it. Recorded here as an observation against this system's inputs, not as a change to System 1's page.

issues.title: Nine signals are already in the dead-letter queue
issues.text: `scored-signals.ams` has 9 messages in state `dead` with 9 matching rows on `scored-signals.ams.dlq`, and `ams-inbound.ams` has 532 dead with 532 on its DLQ. They are visible by design rather than dropped, but nothing routinely inspects them, and a DLQ nobody reads is the same as a discard with extra steps.

issues.title: The gate has never approved a trade at full size
issues.text: 4,153 decisions, 62 approvals — all `REDUCED`, none at full size. 2,719 died at layer `A` because the account is in RECOVERY and 1,100 at sizing for insufficient live statistics. Both are the machinery working correctly. The consequence is that the approve-and-publish path beyond a reduced-size order has never been exercised against a real signal, and layer `J`'s full-cap branch is covered only by tests.

issues.title: Incoming strategies rest on 5–20 trades
issues.text: The three live cells qualified after the out-of-sample gate was lowered to 12 months, and System 1 has no minimum trade-count gate. Their profit factors are small-sample artefacts. This is a knowingly accepted risk on a practice account and explicitly not a reason to refuse orders — but sizing is this system's call, and a thin cell produces an unreliable Kelly fraction. In practice the sizing layer already refuses on insufficient statistics, which is the same protection arriving by a different route.

issues.title: Arriving signals carry no exits
issues.text: All three live map entries have `exits: {}`. Layer `H` reasons about the maximum hold duration against the Friday cutoff, which an empty exit specification does not supply — so it falls back to the configured maximum rather than the strategy's own, and 131 rejections have already landed there.

issues.title: The relay is a stopgap with a defined exit, and it is single-threaded
issues.text: `pubsub_signal_relay.py` polls every 5 seconds with a batch of 10 and no concurrency. That is ample for the current volume of zero, and would be a bottleneck at bar-close bursts across many instruments. Its exit condition is written into its own docstring: when System 2, System 3 and the bridge move to Pub/Sub together, delete it and set `SCORED_SIGNAL_SUB=scored_signal_queue_sub`.
